web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
question: What exact products, subsystems, and engineering workflows does AXISCADES sell today—and how does the post-Akkodis retained core differ from the divested legacy businesses?

epigraph.quote: Do not evaluate a conglomerate on the label on its door; dissect every revenue stream by who signs the cheque, what IP sits inside the box, and whether the contract repeats.
epigraph.author: Forensic Business Analysis Rule

web_blocks.title: The Two-Bucket Architecture: Retained Core Platforms vs. Divested Legacy Services

web_blocks.html: Understanding AXISCADES Technologies in late 2026 requires separating its historical P&L (₹1,159 crore revenue in FY26) from its post-sale retained core [1]. Historically, AXISCADES ran six units: Aerospace, Defence, ESAI (Electronics, Semiconductors, and Artificial Intelligence), Heavy Engineering, Automotive, and Energy [1][2]. By late FY26, the three Core pillars—Aerospace, Defence, and ESAI—drove roughly 78% of sales and earned 15%–24% EBITDA margins [1][3]. By contrast, Heavy Engineering, Automotive, and Energy staffing acted as a low-margin, cash-hungry drag. Mixing high-IP defence gear with routine European auto staffing hid the core's true economics.

Under the ₹2,256 crore (~USD 237 million) Akkodis deal signed in May–June 2026, AXISCADES sold its people-led services [4][5]. It transferred Heavy Engineering, Energy (including EPCOGEN), Automotive (including add solution GmbH's staffing), AXISCADES UK, and AXISCADES Inc. It also sold Aerospace Engineering Services in two steps: 51% in Phase 1 and 49% over 24–30 months in Phase 2 [4][5]. In H1 FY27 (six months ended September 30, 2026), retained units earned ₹378.95 crore, up 55% YoY like-for-like (₹183.4 crore in Q1 and ₹195.6 crore in Q2). Discontinued units added ₹326.81 crore before Phase 1 closed [6][7]. What remains is a focused, IP-led platform across four pillars aimed at flipping the old 80:20 services-to-products mix into 80:20 products-and-solutions by FY30.

web_blocks.title: Segment 1: Defence Electronics, Radars & Counter-Drone Systems (Mistral & ACAT)

web_blocks.html: Defence is AXISCADES' highest-margin and fastest-growing engine. It runs through two units: Mistral Solutions (embedded boards, radar signal processing, and defence computing) and AXISCADES Aerospace & Technologies (ACAT) (system integration, counter-drone gear, and land systems) [8][9]. Instead of billing software hours, this unit wins multi-year 'Make in India' design-and-build orders. Key buyers include DRDO labs (such as LRDE), Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), and the Indian Armed Forces [8][10]. Defence sales jumped over 112% YoY in Q1 FY27 on a retained basis as prototypes entered serial production.

Concrete Example 1 — LLTR Ashwini & Virupaksha AESA Radar Subsystems: DRDO and BEL built India's Low-Level Transportable Radar (LLTR) 'Ashwini' to spot low-flying drones, choppers, and jets. Mistral Solutions won a ~₹100 crore contract to design, ruggedize, and supply its liquid-cooled Signal and Data Processing Units (SDPUs) [8]. A phased-array antenna collects raw radar echoes. Mistral's SDPU reads those multi-gigabit streams in real time, filters out mountain clutter, and runs Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Doppler tracking on custom FPGA/DSP boards. It sends clean target tracks to the command console inside a sealed, liquid-cooled box built for high Himalayan posts. Beyond Ashwini, AXISCADES won orders in a ~₹600 crore radar pipeline. These cover Digital Beam Forming Units for BEL's KUSHA Long Range Battle Management Radar (LRBMR), Digital Transmit/Receive Modules (DTM/DRM), and airborne gear for the Su-30MKI / Virupaksha AESA Radar upgrade [10][11].

Concrete Example 2 — Man-Portable Counter-Drone System (MPCDS) & Land Systems: At the tactical edge, ACAT won direct Indian Army orders for Man-Portable Counter-Drone Systems (MPCDS) [12][13]. A soldier carries the backpack unit to forward posts. Its RF/radar and optical sensors spot rogue quadcopters up to 5 kilometers away. Directional jammers then cut their control and GPS links without firing a shot [13]. On the heavy mechanical side, ACAT builds Tank Transporter Trailers and mobility gear for the Indian Army. However, Q4 FY26 saw ₹142 crore of land-system sales slip into FY27 due to part shortages [4][14].

web_blocks.title: Segment 2: Aerospace Manufacturing, MRO & Global OEM Pedigree

web_blocks.html: AXISCADES' aerospace arm has long anchored its global reach through Tier-1 OEMs like Airbus and Boeing [15]. Under the June 2026 Akkodis deal, the labor-heavy Aerospace Engineering Services unit (stress analysis, CAD design, and seat-by-seat staffing) is moving to Akkodis in two steps (51% upfront, 49% over 24–30 months) [5]. AXISCADES keeps Aerospace Manufacturing, Automated Test Equipment (ATE), and Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul (MRO). This work is centered at the new Devanahalli Atmanirbhar Complex (DAC / Aeroland) near Bengaluru's airport [1][16].

Concrete Example — Automated Test Benches & Precision Aero-Assemblies: Before an avionics box (LRU), flight actuator, or cockpit display goes onto a jet—or returns to service after repair—it must pass strict stress tests. AXISCADES builds custom Automated Test Equipment (ATE) and ground rigs that feed simulated flight loads and sensor signals into the LRU to catch faults. Alongside ATE, Devanahalli is scaling precision sheet-metal, wiring-harness, and structural sub-assemblies for global OEM supply chains. Moving from monthly engineer billing to certified hardware assemblies turns linear headcount into multi-year platform annuities.

web_blocks.title: Segment 3: ESAI (Electronics, Semiconductors & Artificial Intelligence) & Space

web_blocks.html: The ESAI unit—run by Mistral Solutions' commercial team and US-based XiDA Inc.—links silicon, hardware prototyping, and edge AI [1][17]. Unlike pure software IT shops, ESAI runs physical labs with 3D-printed PCB lines and acoustic test chambers [17][18]. Its new sibling, the Space Division at Devanahalli, targets satellite subsystems, payload integration, and space testing for India's growing space sector [5][16].

Concrete Example — Custom Edge-AI & Silicon Reference Boards: Global chipmakers like Altera/Intel and Texas Instruments launch new system-on-chips (SoCs) for robotics, medical imaging, and auto ADAS. OEMs need ready-to-run System-on-Modules (SoMs) and board support packages (BSPs) to test their apps. Mistral/ESAI designs the high-speed multi-layer PCB, adds thermal and power circuits, writes firmware and edge-AI drivers, and checks compliance in-house. It then licenses the design or builds boards in batches [17]. The same precision electronics skill now extends to radiation-tolerant boards for small satellites.

web_blocks.title: Divested Non-Core Segments: Heavy Engineering, Automotive & Energy (Historical Context)

web_blocks.html: To read the 10-year financials in Chapter 6, investors must know what AXISCADES just sold. Until May–October 2026, it ran three non-core service units [4][5]. First was Automotive via Germany's add solution GmbH, writing wiring-harness and embedded code for OEMs like Volkswagen. Second was Energy via EPCOGEN, doing pre-bid FEED design for oil, gas, and renewables. Third was Heavy Engineering, designing off-highway and industrial machines [1][2][9]. Because European auto furloughs and routine drafting squeezed margins, AXISCADES sold these units to Akkodis [1][3]. They remain in historical FY15–FY26 tables, but they are out of the forward compounding engine.

web_blocks.title: The '3% to 97%' Value-Chain Thesis
paragraphs: Management's core thesis is simple: pure design services capture roughly 3% of a defence or aerospace system's lifetime spend, while embedded electronics, subsystems, and serial production capture up to 97% [4]. Every rupee spent at Devanahalli (DAC) and Hyderabad (MAC) aims to move AXISCADES from the 3% design table onto the 97% factory floor.

web_blocks.title: Revenue Visibility & Contract Economics Across the Retained Core

web_blocks.html: Together, the four retained pillars give AXISCADES an FY27 revenue bridge of ₹1,377 crore across three layers [14]. About ₹927 crore sits in hard orders on the books, including ₹142 crore of land-system deliveries deferred from Q4 FY26. Another ₹284–₹285 crore comes from sole-source or limited-source OEM forecasts. Roughly ₹165 crore comes from acquisition-linked sales in ESAI and aero manufacturing [14]. Repeatability varies by unit: Mistral's radar SDPUs and beam formers track multi-year DRDO/BEL tranches, aero ATE and MRO earn lifecycle fees, and ESAI boards follow global chip cycles.

For an equity underwriter, the main takeaway is clear. AXISCADES' retained core is no longer a commodity staffing shop. Whether it is a liquid-cooled SDPU in an Ashwini radar, a counter-drone jammer on a border post, an avionics test bench for Airbus/Boeing, or an edge-AI module for a US chipmaker, each retained product sits at a certified bottleneck. Switching vendors at that stage is slow and costly.

At the same time, exiting Heavy Engineering, Automotive, and Energy focuses sales onto fewer large buyers. In Defence, DRDO labs, Bharat Electronics (BEL), HAL, and the Indian Army drive most domestic orders. In Aerospace Manufacturing and MRO, Airbus and Boeing anchor the pipeline. In ESAI, a few global chip leaders drive board wins [1][8][15]. That focus cuts both ways: 10–20 year radar and jet programs give multi-year visibility once qualified, yet a delay in one major MoD tender or Airbus rate plan hits quarterly plant load right away.

Investors should also watch how the Space unit matures across FY27–FY29. Management built dedicated clean-room and test bays at Devanahalli for satellite subsystems [5][16]. Still, Space is early-stage compared with Defence and Aerospace. Winning repeat private-constellation or ISRO payload orders without heavy upfront R&D burn will decide if this fourth pillar adds real margin or drains cash.

book_paragraphs: To understand what we are really underwriting in AXISCADES Technologies, we must look past its old corporate brochure. For most of the past decade, the firm looked like a six-headed hydra: Aerospace, Defence, Semiconductors and AI, Heavy Engineering, Automotive, and Energy. In FY26, that combined machine posted ₹1,159 crore in sales. Yet roughly 78% of the business—Aerospace, Defence, and ESAI—carried the growth and earned 15% to 24% operating margins. The other 22% in European auto staffing, heavy machinery design, and oil-and-gas engineering was cyclical and dragged margins down. Separating those two pieces is the first step in judging what the business is worth.

With the ₹2,256 crore Akkodis deal signed in May and June 2026, AXISCADES performed surgery on itself. It sold Heavy Engineering, Energy (including EPCOGEN), Automotive, and the labor-heavy part of Aerospace Engineering Services. It kept what rivals cannot easily copy: Defence Electronics, Aerospace Manufacturing and MRO, ESAI, and a new Space arm. In H1 FY27, those retained continuing operations earned ₹378.95 crore—up 55% year-on-year—while sold units added ₹326.81 crore before Phase 1 closed. Let us walk through each retained pillar with a concrete example so you can see how each rupee is earned. Each of those four pillars relies on certified hardware or deep domain IP rather than generic billing hours.

First, consider Defence Electronics and Systems inside Mistral Solutions and ACAT. When DRDO and Bharat Electronics build a battlefield radar like the Ashwini Low-Level Transportable Radar, the dish is only half the system. The brain is the liquid-cooled Signal and Data Processing Unit that turns raw echoes into target tracks for fighters, choppers, and drones. Mistral won roughly ₹100 crore to build those ruggedized processors. It also sits inside a ₹600 crore pipeline spanning Digital Beam Forming Units for the Kusha radar and gear for the Su-30MKI Virupaksha AESA upgrade. Meanwhile, ACAT builds backpack Man-Portable Counter-Drone Systems for the Indian Army that spot rogue drones five kilometers out and jam their links, alongside tank transporter trailers.

Second, look at Aerospace Manufacturing and MRO. While Akkodis takes over seat-by-seat structural design staffing in two tranches, AXISCADES keeps its Devanahalli Atmanirbhar Complex near Bengaluru airport. There it builds Automated Test Equipment, ground rigs, and certified aero-assemblies for Airbus and Boeing. Instead of billing an engineer's hourly wage, the firm gets paid for certified hardware that validates avionics before flight. That shift moves the company from linear headcount billing toward multi-year platform annuities.

Third, there is ESAI—Electronics, Semiconductors, and Artificial Intelligence—plus the new Space arm. Through Mistral and US unit XiDA, AXISCADES designs high-speed printed circuit boards, writes low-level firmware, and builds edge-AI reference modules for chipmakers like Altera and Texas Instruments. It backs this work with in-house 3D-printed PCB lines and acoustic labs. That same precision electronics skill now supports satellite payload testing and space subsystems at Devanahalli.

Finally, remember why legacy units—like add solution GmbH serving Volkswagen in Germany or EPCOGEN serving oil refineries—had to go. They were respectable shops, but they trapped talent in low-margin hourly billing and European auto furloughs. By shedding them, AXISCADES is betting its future on moving from the 3% design table to the 97% manufacturing and IP floor. That strategic trade-off sets the stage for the margin and cash-flow shift we examine next.

book_subsections.title: Why Segment Mix Determines Cash Conversion
paragraphs: Not all retained units behave the same way on the balance sheet. ESAI reference boards and commercial aero test benches usually follow standard industrial payment terms. By contrast, Indian Army land systems (like tank trailers) and DPSU radar subsystems require multi-stage checks and milestone billing. As you read Chapters 3 and 6, keep that mix tension in mind. The faster Mistral's electronics and ESAI grow compared with heavy mechanical work, the cleaner AXISCADES' margins and cash flow will get.

The post-Akkodis revenue reset matters just as much. Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the Akkodis deal remove roughly ₹650 crore of annual services revenue. As a result, FY27 and FY28 will look smaller on a raw headline basis before Devanahalli and Hyderabad ramp up. Separating continuing operations from discontinued units is the only way to track the true core.

book_subsections.title: Walking the Factory Floor: From Design Table to Certified Hardware
paragraphs: Let us picture what happens inside AXISCADES' Bengaluru and Hyderabad plants so these segment names feel concrete. In the Mistral lab, an FPGA engineer is not writing routine business software. They are laying out a 16-layer circuit board that must survive -40°C Himalayan winters and heavy electromagnetic noise inside a fighter or mobile radar. Once that board passes DRDO's stress screening, Mistral does not just hand over a drawing—it ships the sealed, liquid-cooled Signal and Data Processing Unit in serial batches.

Over at the Devanahalli Atmanirbhar Complex near Bengaluru airport, the work shifts to aerospace hardware and Automated Test Equipment. When an airline or defence depot pulls an avionics box off a jet for service, technicians plug it into an AXISCADES test rig that mimics altitude, power swings, and sensor data. Building that rig takes deep Airbus and Boeing platform know-how, and maintaining it creates sticky, repeat revenue.

Meanwhile, in ESAI and Space, engineers work with US unit XiDA and global chip partners to build edge-AI modules and radiation-tolerant satellite electronics. Across all four retained pillars—Defence, Aerospace Manufacturing and MRO, ESAI, and Space—the common thread is physical certification. You cannot hand a flight-qualified radar processor or an AS9100 test bench to the cheapest hourly bidder overnight. That is why the retained core has a much higher quality ceiling than the staffing units it just sold.

book_subsections.title: Checking the FY27 Revenue Bridge Pillar by Pillar
paragraphs: Before we turn to unit economics in Chapter 3, let us anchor management's FY27 retained-business bridge of ₹1,377 crore. Roughly ₹927 crore is hard orders already on the books, including ₹142 crore of defence land-system deliveries delayed from Q4 FY26 due to part shortages. Another ₹284 to ₹285 crore comes from sole-source or limited-source OEM forecasts where AXISCADES is already qualified, and ₹165 crore reflects acquisition-linked additions in ESAI and aero manufacturing. Over two-thirds of the retained FY27 target is backed by signed contracts, though shipping those orders on time remains the key test.

book_subsections.title: The Concentration Trade-Off: Fewer Customers, Deeper Roots
paragraphs: There is one more trade-off to grasp about the post-Akkodis business. When AXISCADES sold Heavy Engineering, Automotive, and Energy, it traded hundreds of mid-sized industrial and European auto clients for deeper focus on a smaller set of sovereign and Tier-1 aerospace buyers: DRDO, Bharat Electronics, HAL, the Indian Army, Airbus, Boeing, and global chip leaders. In strong years, that focus is a superpower—programs like the Su-30MKI Virupaksha radar upgrade or Airbus jets run for ten years or more with repeat orders and high switching costs.

In slower years, however, concentration means you cannot hide behind a dozen other sectors if one major defence tender stalls or a jet program slows. And as the new Space unit ramps up at Devanahalli, we must watch whether satellite testing wins profitable orders rather than turning into an open-ended R&D drain. Grasping both the stickiness of certified hardware and the lumpiness of large institutional buyers is vital before we examine Chapter 3's cash waterfall.

book_callouts.title: Separating Continuing from Discontinued DNA
book_callouts.text: When analyzing FY27 and beyond, never extrapolate the old ₹1,159 crore consolidated revenue base blindly. Roughly half of H1 FY27 group revenue came from units moving to Akkodis; the true compounder test applies only to the ₹379 crore H1 retained core.
